analysis.one_liner: Requires defense contractors to share repair parts, tools, and information with the military.
analysis.headline: The bill has been referred to the House Armed Services Committee and has not moved since its September 4 introduction, with 5 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Defense Department from signing procurement contracts unless the contractor agrees in writing to give the military fair and reasonable access to the parts, tools, and information needed to diagnose, maintain, and repair the equipment it buys — at prices no worse than what authorized repair shops pay. It also directs the Defense Secretary to review existing contracts and work to strip intellectual-property restrictions that block military mechanics from doing repairs themselves, and requires a Government Accountability Office report on compliance a year after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Military service members and Defense Department maintenance crews, who could fix equipment using their own depots and mechanics instead of waiting for manufacturer-authorized service. Taxpayers also benefit, since the Pentagon often pays premium manufacturer prices for repairs it could perform itself, and lawmakers of both parties have cited long repair delays that leave equipment out of service.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members, military mechanics, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires that every new defense procurement contract include written terms giving the Defense Department access to the same parts, tools, and repair information the manufacturer gives its authorized repair providers, at no worse prices [S2].

It defines 'fair and reasonable access' to include equivalent prices, terms, delivery, and rights of use compared to what authorized repair providers receive, and requires government-determined fair pricing when a manufacturer offers nothing to anyone [S2].
It directs the Secretary of Defense to review existing contracts for intellectual-property constraints that block military maintenance and to identify modifications needed to remove them [S2].
It requires a Comptroller General report to Congress on Defense Department compliance within one year, creating oversight [S2].
Contractors cannot simply abandon existing programs: the waiver authority for pre-existing programs requires an independent technical risk assessment and justification submitted to Congress [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and original equipment manufacturers that now sell repair parts, tools, and software exclusively on their own terms. They would lose a portion of their aftermarket revenue and their leverage to steer repairs through authorized channels at premium prices, and they would have to share diagnostic software and pairing tools they currently hold back.

drawbacks.text: Contractors argue that required access to repair materials can raise upfront procurement prices or expose sensitive technical data and software, and the bill itself acknowledges this by requiring a technical risk assessment and cost, schedule, and performance analysis before waiving the requirement for existing programs [S2].

The bill applies only to future Defense Department contracts unless agencies affirmatively renegotiate, so current equipment could stay locked under manufacturer control for years, with waivers available for any pre-existing program [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is straightforward: the military already owns the equipment, and giving its own mechanics the parts, tools, and manuals to fix it reduces repair delays and premium manufacturer charges. The main honest cost is that some contracts may carry higher upfront prices if contractors no longer recoup costs through the repair monopoly, and sensitive systems will need careful handling. The bill tries to manage this by pricing access at the same rates authorized repair shops get and requiring risk assessments before waiving requirements for legacy programs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Armed Services Committee, which has taken no further action on it so far; it is waiting to see whether it gets a hearing, a markup, or a slot in the annual defense authorization bill.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the bill on September 4, 2025, joined at introduction by Rep. Jennifer Kiggans, a Republican from Virginia, and Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat [S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services, and no further action has been recorded since [S4].
The bill has 5 cosponsors, split between the parties, with 2 Republicans and 3 Democrats listed [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, defense equipment manufacturers keep their exclusive control over repair parts, tools, and information, and taxpayers keep paying manufacturer-set repair prices, because the bill has not advanced past committee referral.

industries.industry: Defense equipment manufacturers (original equipment makers of military electronics and vehicles)
industries.note: These contractors currently control the parts, tools, and software needed to fix the equipment they sell the Pentagon, and can charge premium prices or route repairs through authorized channels. The bill would force them to offer those materials to the government at no worse terms than authorized repair shops get, cutting into their aftermarket revenue.

industries.industry: Independent repair providers and military maintenance depots
industries.note: Government and private repair shops would gain legal access to parts, diagnostic software, and pairing tools they are often locked out of, letting them compete to service equipment the military already owns. This shortens repair delays for service members and cuts costs for taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: This bill is at the stage where most bills stall: referred to the House Armed Services Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled. Its realistic path to becoming law is as a provision in the annual National Defense Authorization Act, where right-to-repair language has previously drawn interest; as a standalone bill it is likely to sit in committee unless that happens.
